June 15, 2026
Mehmet Oz, MD
Administrator
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)
Department of Health and Human Services
Attention: CMS-0062-P
Mail Stop C4-26-05
7500 Security Boulevard
Baltimore, MD 21244-1850
Submitted electronically via: https://www.regulations.gov/
Re: CMS-0062-P â€“ 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Proposed Rule
Dear Administrator Oz:
Smart Health Network (SHN) respectfully submits these comments in response to the Centers 
for Medicare & Medicaid Servicesâ€™ (CMS) 2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P), published in the Federal Register on 
April 14, 2026. The public comment period closes today, June 15, 2026.
Smart Health Network is a mission-locked, neutral infrastructure initiative designed to serve as 
common rails for health data exchangeâ€”operated in the public interest, governed by a Public 
Benefit Corporation, and built expressly to address the architecture and institutional 
fragmentation that prevents American healthcare from functioning efficiently. Our network is 
designed as an NÃ—1 substrate: every participant connects once and reaches the entire network, 
while patient data stays where it lives, and the patient remains at the architectural center with 
meaningful control over their own information.
SHN applauds CMS for the bold and necessary direction reflected in CMS-0062-P. We view this 
rulemaking as a critical extension of the foundation established in CMS-0057-F and offer 
substantive comments on four priority areas where we believe our operational experience and 
mission perspective can meaningfully contribute to the record.
I. SHN Is Actively Implementing CMS-0057-F FHIR Standards for Prior 
Authorization
Smart Health Network was designed from its inception to operate on the FHIR-based 
interoperability standards that CMS has mandated through its prior rulemakings, including the 
Prior Authorization API requirements finalized in CMS-0057-F. The architecture underlying SHN 
is purpose-built to leverage the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci Implementation Guidesâ€”including the 
Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), and 
Prior Authorization Support (PAS) implementation guidesâ€”as the native exchange standards 
for prior authorization workflows.
The promise of these standards is one SHN takes seriously: a physician office submits a prior 
authorization request once, through a single connection; the payerâ€™s system retrieves the clinical 
documentation it needs directly and electronically, without fax or manual intervention; the patient 
sees the request status in real time; and the decision returns in a fraction of the time currently 
required. This is not aspirational for SHNâ€”it is the operational model we are building toward in 
our initial Delaware deployment.
We therefore strongly support CMSâ€™s proposal in Section II.A.4 to formally require the CRD and 
DTR Implementation Guides for the Prior Authorization API by October 1, 2027. We concur with 
the position advanced by HL7 International that the Prior Authorization Support (PAS) IG should 
be included alongside CRD and DTR as a required standard, as PAS provides the end-to-end 
prior authorization exchange capability that completes the workflow and avoids leaving 
implementers with a partial technical toolset.
SHN also affirms that requiring conformance with unexpired versions of these IGsâ€”rather than 
pinning to specific version numbersâ€”is the correct regulatory approach. Version pinning risks 
creating a regulatory floor that quickly becomes a ceiling, preventing adoption of material 
improvements that the HL7 community regularly produces. We recommend CMS clarify in the 
final rule, consistent with HL7â€™s recommendation, that prior to January 1, 2028, impacted payers 
retain flexibility to implement the version of the IG best suited to their state of readiness for the 
CMS-0057-F compliance timeline, and that the January 1, 2028 date serves as the convergence 
point to the most current unexpired versions.
On compliance timing, SHN notes that the October 1, 2027 deadline for requiring additional 
implementation guides falls at the end of a fiscal yearâ€”a period of significant operational 
burden for payers managing enrollment, renewals, and budget cycles. We echo the 
recommendation in HL7â€™s comment that an end of Q1 2028 date would allow meaningful and 
thorough implementation while achieving the same policy objective. We urge CMS to give 
serious weight to this alignment in the final rule.
II. SHN Supports FHIR-Based Electronic Prior Authorization for Medical 
Benefit Drug Claims, Including an Integrated Pharmacy and Prior Auth 
Approach
SHN is strongly supportive of CMSâ€™s proposal in Section II.B.3 to require impacted payers to 
incorporate drugs covered under a medical benefit into the Prior Authorization API by October 1, 
2027. This proposal addresses a long-standing gap: the current regulatory framework has 
created a bifurcated system in which drugs processed as medical claimsâ€”often high-cost 
biologics, infused therapies, and oncology agents administered in clinical settingsâ€”fall outside 
the electronic prior authorization infrastructure that CMS has been building for non-drug items 
and services.
From SHNâ€™s perspective, this bifurcation is architecturally unnecessary and clinically harmful. 
When a physician orders a drug that will be administered in an infusion suite and billed under 
the medical benefit, the clinical documentation requirements for prior authorization are 
substantively identical to those for other complex services. There is no principled reason to 
process this request through fax, portal, or phone when a FHIR-based API workflow using CRD, 
DTR, PAS, and CDex can accomplish the same result electronically, with greater speed, lower 
administrative burden, and full auditability.
We support using the system through which claims are processed as the primary categorization 
principle for determining whether the Prior Authorization API or NCPDP standards apply. This 
approach respects the operational reality that medical benefit drugs flow through different claims 
adjudication infrastructure than pharmacy benefit drugs, and it provides implementers with a 
workable bright-line rule. We do recommend that CMS provide additional sub-regulatory 
guidance identifying the most common drug categories that would fall within the medical benefit 
scope, to reduce implementation ambiguity particularly for smaller payers and state Medicaid 
programs.
Toward an Integrated FHIR Approach for Pharmacy Claims
Looking beyond the immediate proposal, SHN encourages CMS to establish a longer-horizon 
policy signal toward a more unified, FHIR-based approach for pharmacy claims and pharmacy 
prior authorization. We recognize that the NCPDP SCRIPT and Real-Time Prescription Benefit 
(RTPB) standards are mature, widely deployed, and technically sound for pharmacy benefit 
drug workflows. We are not recommending that CMS mandate replacement of these standards 
in this rulemaking.
However, the healthcare system will best serve patients if the longer-term regulatory trajectory 
moves toward a single interoperability substrate rather than two parallel but non-interoperable 
systems. As FHIR-based standards matureâ€”including through ongoing HL7 work to align the 
CRD and RTPB use casesâ€”CMS should actively monitor the readiness of FHIR-based 
alternatives for pharmacy prior authorization and commit in sub-regulatory guidance to a future 
rulemaking process that would address this convergence.
SHN specifically supports CMSâ€™s request for comment in Section II.A.2 on whether the NCPDP 
RTPB standard could negate the need for the NCPDP F&B standard for electronic prior 
authorization. Our view is that real-time, patient-specific coverage information provided by 
RTPB is superior to group-level formulary files for the purpose of determining whether prior 
authorization is required at the point of prescribing. CMS should give serious consideration to 
elevating RTPB as the preferred standard for formulary discovery in the electronic prior 
authorization workflow, while recognizing that full integration with FHIR-based medical benefit 
workflows remains the long-term goal.
We also support the proposal to require payers to include prior authorization information for 
drugs in the Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs by October 1, 2027 
(Section II.F.1.b). Giving patients and providers a consistent, complete view of prior 
authorization status across both drug and non-drug items through the same API infrastructure is 
a meaningful step toward the transparent, patient-centered system SHN is built to support.
III. An API Endpoint Directory Is Critically Needed: SHN Urges CMS to 
Proceed with This Infrastructure
Among the proposals in CMS-0062-P, SHN views the API endpoint reporting and publication 
requirements in Section II.E as among the most consequential for the long-term functioning of 
the interoperability ecosystem. We strongly support this proposal and urge CMS to finalize it in 
its most comprehensive form.
The absence of a centralized, authoritative, machine-readable directory of payer API endpoints 
is one of the most underappreciated structural barriers to interoperability in American healthcare 
today. Every electronic health record vendor, every third-party application developer, every 
payer technical team that attempts to implement the FHIR-based APIs CMS has mandated 
must discover, validate, and maintain connections to hundreds of payer endpointsâ€”a process 
that is currently manual, error-prone, and enormously duplicative. Without a standardized 
directory, the NÃ—1 connectivity model that makes shared infrastructure valuable cannot be 
achieved; instead, the ecosystem defaults to the NÃ—N bilateral connectivity model that has 
produced decades of fragmentation.
SHNâ€™s own architecture demonstrates why endpoint directory infrastructure matters: our 
network is designed so that a provider or patient app connects once to SHN and can reach any 
participating payer, not because we have built bilateral connections to each payer, but because 
a common directory and routing layer eliminates the need for each participant to discover and 
maintain those connections independently. CMSâ€™s proposed endpoint registry would provide a 
public-sector analog to this function, and SHN is prepared to align our own directory 
infrastructure with whatever federal standard CMS adopts.
Recommendation: Adopt the FAST National Directory (NDH) IG as the Required 
Reporting Standard
SHN endorses HL7â€™s recommendation that CMS formally require the FAST National Directory 
(NDH) Implementation Guide as the standard framework for endpoint registration, reporting, and 
discovery. The NDH IG was designed precisely for this purpose: to create a scalable, FHIR-
native, semantically consistent directory that goes beyond simple URL collection to capture the 
full set of metadata necessary for automated endpoint discovery and trust verification.
We recommend that, at minimum, the endpoint directory capture the following information for 
each payer API:
â€¢
The FHIR capability statement URL for each interoperability API
â€¢
Authorization server metadata, including OAuth 2.0 server discovery endpoints
â€¢
Digital certificates and certificate authority information
â€¢
Dynamic Client Registration endpoints where supported
â€¢
Supported FHIR implementation guide versions for each API
â€¢
Trust framework participation attestations
â€¢
Contact information for technical onboarding support
We support CMSâ€™s proposed requirement that payers report this information within 60 days of 
the final ruleâ€™s effective date and update CMS within one week of material changes. We also 
support requiring new payers to register at least 60 days before beginning coverage, so that the 
directory is prospective rather than retrospective.
On the question of publication format, SHN recommends that CMS publish the endpoint registry 
as a FHIR-enabled API, not merely as a machine-readable flat file. A queryable FHIR API would 
allow EHR vendors, app developers, and network operators like SHN to automate endpoint 
discovery rather than batch-downloading and manually processing a static file. The investment 
in a FHIR-native registry infrastructure will compound over time as the number of participants, 
APIs, and use cases grows.
We note that the burden on payers to report this information is minimal relative to the substantial 
benefits to the entire ecosystem. The proposed requirement to update within one week of 
changes appropriately ensures the directory remains current without imposing continuous 
monitoring obligations. SHN encourages CMS to also establish a public-facing status 
mechanismâ€”whether through a health check API or a validated endpoint testing toolâ€”so that 
the directory can be operationally validated, not just administratively maintained.
IV. SHN Supports the Security Outcomes the FAST Security IG Is Designed 
to Deliver, and Urges an Outcomes-Based Adoption Framework
Smart Health Network supports CMSâ€™s recommendation of the FAST Security Implementation 
Guide (IG) in Section II.A.5 and agrees that the security architecture underlying the 
interoperability system CMS is building is foundationalâ€”as important as the clinical data 
standards themselves. A system in which organizational identity cannot be verified, access 
cannot be reliably authorized, and credentials cannot be revoked in a timely way will not achieve 
the trust necessary for broad participation. SHN therefore strongly supports the security 
objectives the FAST Security IG is designed to guarantee.
At the same time, SHN urges CMS to frame any future requirement in terms of the security 
outcomes those objectives represent, rather than by the specific trust topology the current IG 
presupposes. This distinction matters at national scale.
The Security Outcomes That Must Be Guaranteed
The three core assurances that any conforming implementation should be required to deliver 
are:
â€¢
Verifiable organizational identity: a relying party must be able to confirm, through a 
mechanism that is independently auditable and not solely self-asserted, that the entity 
requesting or receiving data is who it claims to be.
â€¢
Authenticated and authorized access: every API transaction must be preceded by 
authentication of the requesting entity and a determination that the entity is authorized to 
receive the requested data for the stated purpose.
â€¢
Timely revocation: when an organizationâ€™s authorization to participate is suspended or 
terminated, that change must propagate through the system within a defined and 
enforceable timeframe such that stale credentials cannot be used to obtain access.
The FAST Security IG provides one well-reasoned path to achieving these outcomes. Its 
mechanismsâ€”OAuth authorization servers issuing access tokens, X.509 certificate chains 
anchored to a trust-community certificate authority, and participation governance through 
shared legal agreementsâ€”are technically sound and appropriate for many implementers. SHN 
does not oppose their use and recognizes that for the majority of the impacted payer 
community, the IGâ€™s architecture is a practical and deployable solution.
The Case for Technology-Neutral, Outcomes-Based Adoption
However, codifying the IGâ€™s specific centralized topology as the exclusive conformance path 
would foreclose functionally equivalent architectures that achieve the same three assurances 
through different means. In particular, it would foreclose decentralized and cryptographically 
verifiable models in which:
â€¢
Authorization travels as a portable, independently verifiable signed artifactâ€”a credential 
or token that carries its own proof of issuance and scopeâ€”rather than being issued by a 
server that must be queried for each transaction.
â€¢
Trust is anchored in a published, append-only directory of organizational signing keys 
rather than a single certificate authority, removing the single point of failure that a 
centralized CA represents for national infrastructure.
â€¢
Revocation is implemented through short-lived credentials or verifiable revocation 
registries rather than Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) or Certificate Revocation 
List (CRL) lookups that depend on CA availability.
These are not theoretical alternatives. Decentralized identity and verifiable credential 
architectures are in production use in financial services, government identity programs, and 
cross-border data exchange contexts. They can satisfy the three security outcomes listed above 
and, in some respects, do so more resiliently than centralized PKI at scale. SHNâ€™s own 
architecture incorporates elements of this approach, and we have a direct interest in ensuring 
the regulatory framework does not inadvertently mandate a topology that is incompatible with 
architectures CMS has not yet evaluated.
Recommended Framing for the Final Rule and Future Rulemaking
SHN recommends that CMS adopt the following approach to FAST Security IG adoption:
â€¢
In this final rule: formally recommend the FAST Security IG v2.0.0 as a reference 
implementation of the security outcomes framework, while making clear that 
recommendation of the IG does not imply that the IGâ€™s specific trust topology is the only 
acceptable conformance path.
â€¢
In sub-regulatory guidance: publish explicit, measurable criteria for the three security 
outcomesâ€”verifiable organizational identity, authenticated and authorized access, and 
timely revocationâ€”against which both IG-conformant implementations and alternative 
implementations can be evaluated.
â€¢
In a subsequent rulemaking proposing to require security standards: frame the 
requirement as outcomes-based, requiring that implementers demonstrate they meet the 
published criteria and can interoperate with IG-conformant partners, while expressly 
permitting alternative implementations that achieve the same verifiable assurances.
This approach preserves the trust and scale the FAST Security IG is designed to deliver, 
advances adoption of a well-tested reference framework, and avoids mandating a single 
centralized topology for infrastructure that will serve hundreds of millions of patients and 
thousands of organizations over decades. It also positions the regulatory framework to 
accommodate the genuine innovation in decentralized identity and cryptographic trust that is 
likely to mature significantly over the timeframe in which these requirements will be operative.
On the specific question of Tiered OAuth: SHN supports CMSâ€™s consideration of Tiered OAuth 
as a mechanism for organizational-level authentication where the IGâ€™s topology is in use. We 
recommend, consistent with the outcomes-based framing above, that any Tiered OAuth 
requirement specify the authorization delegation and cross-network routing outcomes it is 
intended to achieve, and expressly permit alternative token and credential formats that satisfy 
those outcomes, rather than requiring a specific OAuth profile implementation.
SHN also supports the proposal to align endpoint directory metadata in Section II.E with security 
metadataâ€”including authorization server endpoints, supported authentication methods, and 
trust framework participationâ€”so that the directory enables automated onboarding and trusted 
exchange. We recommend that the metadata schema for the directory be defined in a manner 
that accommodates both centralized OAuth server discovery and decentralized key directory 
models, so that the directory itself does not inadvertently encode a topology requirement that 
the security standard does not.
V. Conclusion
Smart Health Network appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on CMS-0062-P. The 
proposals in this rule represent meaningful, necessary progress toward the interoperability 
infrastructure American healthcare has long needed. The mandatory adoption of prior 
authorization implementation guides, the extension of FHIR-based workflows to medical benefit 
drug claims, the creation of a national API endpoint directory, and the formal recognition of the 
FAST Security IG each address structural gaps that have perpetuated fragmentation, 
administrative waste, and delayed patient care.
SHNâ€™s specific recommendations are summarized below:
â€¢
Finalize the requirement for CRD, DTR, and PAS implementation guides for the Prior 
Authorization API, with a compliance date aligned to the end of Q1 2028 to avoid overlap 
with year-end operational cycles.
â€¢
Require impacted payers to include drugs covered under the medical benefit in the Prior 
Authorization API by October 1, 2027, with supporting sub-regulatory guidance on 
categorization edge cases.
â€¢
Signal a long-term policy direction toward FHIR-based convergence for pharmacy prior 
authorization workflows, while maintaining NCPDP standards for the near term.
â€¢
Finalize the API endpoint reporting requirements and publish the registry as a queryable 
FHIR API, adopting the FAST NDH IG as the required reporting standard with metadata 
that accommodates both centralized and decentralized trust models.
â€¢
Formally recommend the FAST Security IG v2.0.0 as a reference implementation of the 
security outcomes framework, publish explicit measurable criteria for verifiable 
organizational identity, authenticated and authorized access, and timely revocation, and 
frame any future requirement as outcomes-based rather than topology-specific.
â€¢
Align endpoint directory metadata requirements with security metadata to support 
automated onboarding, while ensuring the schema accommodates both OAuth server 
discovery and decentralized key directory models.
SHN stands ready to serve as a demonstration partner for many of these proposals and 
welcomes ongoing dialogue with CMS and ONC about how neutral, mission-locked network 
infrastructure can complement and accelerate the interoperability goals reflected in this 
rulemaking.
Respectfully submitted,
Smart Health Network
Public Benefit Corporation
June 15, 2026
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Smart Health Network (SHN), Public Benefit Corporation.
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor; Other neutral health data exchange infrastructure.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** SHN states it is building mission-locked, neutral common rails for health data exchange and implementing FHIR-based prior authorization infrastructure in an initial Delaware deployment.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

SHN strongly supports CMS-0062-P as a continuation of CMS-0057-F and endorses mandatory FHIR-based prior authorization standards, inclusion of medical benefit drugs, and creation of a national API endpoint directory. It asks CMS to require CRD, DTR, and PAS; use unexpired IG versions with a Q1 2028 convergence date; adopt FAST NDH for endpoint reporting; and treat FAST Security as an outcomes-based framework rather than a mandate for one centralized trust topology.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; PRIVACY-SECURITY-related implementation within GENERAL; PATIENT-ACCESS/API expansion; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS indirectly through national FHIR PA infrastructure.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations are cited directly; the comment references CMS-0062-P, CMS-0057-F, Section II.A.4, Section II.B.3, Section II.A.2, Section II.F.1.b, Section II.E, and Section II.A.5.
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR; Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS, and CDex IGs; NCPDP SCRIPT; NCPDP RTPB; NCPDP Formulary & Benefit; FAST National Directory (NDH) IG; FAST Security IG v2.0.0; OAuth 2.0; Tiered OAuth; X.509 certificates; Dynamic Client Registration; FHIR CapabilityStatement; decentralized identity; verifiable credentials.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Mandatory prior authorization IGs**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** SHN is actively building on CRD, DTR, and PAS and argues that PAS completes the end-to-end prior authorization workflow.
- **Specific request:** Require CRD, DTR, and PAS for the Prior Authorization API, not only CRD and DTR.

**Topic 2: Versioning and compliance date**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Pinning to specific versions could freeze implementers on outdated specifications, while the October 1, 2027 deadline overlaps payer year-end operational cycles.
- **Specific request:** Require conformance with unexpired IG versions, allow pre-2028 flexibility, use January 1, 2028 as a convergence point, and consider end of Q1 2028 as the compliance date.

**Topic 3: Medical benefit drugs in the Prior Authorization API**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Medical benefit drugs, including infused therapies, biologics, and oncology agents, require similar documentation to other complex services and should not remain on fax, portal, or phone workflows.
- **Specific request:** Finalize inclusion of medical benefit drugs in the Prior Authorization API and issue sub-regulatory guidance on common categories and edge cases.

**Topic 4: Pharmacy benefit direction and RTPB**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** NCPDP standards are mature for current pharmacy workflows, but patients would benefit from eventual convergence toward a single FHIR interoperability substrate.
- **Specific request:** Maintain NCPDP standards for now, signal future FHIR convergence, monitor FHIR pharmacy PA readiness, and consider RTPB as superior to group-level formulary files for identifying PA needs at prescribing.

**Topic 5: API endpoint directory**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Lack of a centralized, authoritative, machine-readable endpoint directory creates manual, duplicative, error-prone connection work and perpetuates N-by-N fragmentation.
- **Specific request:** Finalize comprehensive endpoint reporting, require FAST NDH IG, publish the registry as a queryable FHIR API, and include technical/security metadata.

**Topic 6: FAST Security and trust architecture**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** SHN supports the security outcomes FAST Security is designed to achieve but argues exclusive adoption of a centralized trust topology could block functionally equivalent decentralized approaches.
- **Specific request:** Recommend FAST Security IG v2.0.0 as a reference implementation, publish measurable outcomes for identity, authorization, and revocation, and permit alternative implementations that interoperate and meet those outcomes.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** SHN supports requiring implementation guides for the Prior Authorization API and specifically asks CMS to require CRD, DTR, and PAS.
- **S2:** SHN supports requiring unexpired versions rather than pinning fixed version numbers.
- **S3:** SHN recommends version transition flexibility before January 1, 2028 and a convergence point to the most current unexpired versions.
- **S12:** SHN supports medical benefit drug PA through FHIR APIs and states that CRD, DTR, PAS, and CDex can support the workflow electronically.
- **S15:** SHN supports using the claims-processing system as the primary distinction between medical and pharmacy benefit drugs and asks CMS for sub-regulatory guidance on common categories.
- **S21:** SHN supports the policy but recommends shifting the compliance date to the end of Q1 2028 because October 1, 2027 falls during a high-burden payer operational period.
- **S25:** SHN views RTPB as superior to group-level formulary files for determining whether PA is required at prescribing, while recognizing NCPDP standards remain mature and appropriate near term.
- **S26:** SHN recommends publishing the endpoint registry as a queryable FHIR API instead of only a flat machine-readable file.
- **S27:** SHN supports reporting within 60 days of the final rule effective date, updates within one week of material changes, and registration by new payers at least 60 days before coverage begins.
- **S23/S24:** SHN recommends endpoint reporting include capability statement URLs, OAuth server metadata, certificates, Dynamic Client Registration endpoints, supported IG versions, trust framework attestations, and technical contacts.
- **S33:** SHN supports public publication of the endpoint registry and recommends a health check API or validated endpoint testing tool so the directory is operationally validated.
- **S44-S50:** SHN indirectly addresses FHIR suitability, coexistence with other standards, timeline, cost-benefit, and standards maturity by supporting FHIR for medical benefit PA and longer-term pharmacy convergence while preserving mature NCPDP workflows now.
- **S66-S82:** SHN provides broader infrastructure recommendations on security, trust, endpoint routing, and network architecture.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize CRD, DTR, and PAS as required Prior Authorization API implementation guides.
2. Require conformance with unexpired IG versions and avoid fixed version pinning.
3. Clarify pre-2028 implementation flexibility and consider end of Q1 2028 as the compliance date.
4. Include medical benefit drugs in the Prior Authorization API by the final compliance date.
5. Provide sub-regulatory guidance on medical versus pharmacy benefit categorization edge cases.
6. Maintain NCPDP pharmacy standards near term while signaling longer-term FHIR convergence.
7. Consider RTPB the preferred standard for formulary discovery in ePA workflows.
8. Require payer API endpoint reporting and publish a national endpoint directory.
9. Adopt FAST NDH IG as the endpoint reporting standard.
10. Publish the endpoint registry as a queryable FHIR API with operational health validation.
11. Include security metadata in endpoint directory reporting.
12. Recommend FAST Security IG v2.0.0 as a reference implementation, but define conformance around measurable security outcomes.
13. Permit decentralized identity, verifiable credential, or alternative trust approaches if they satisfy identity, authorization, revocation, and interoperability criteria.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Incomplete PA IG requirements, endpoint discovery fragmentation, ambiguity in drug benefit categorization, premature topology-specific security mandates, and bifurcated FHIR/NCPDP infrastructure.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Continued fax/portal/phone workflows, duplicative endpoint maintenance, fragmentation, slower PA decisions, barriers to scalable network infrastructure, and foreclosed innovation in trust models.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Payer year-end operational burden, manual endpoint discovery, lack of authoritative directory metadata, version-transition complexity, pharmacy/medical benefit categorization ambiguity, and centralized trust single points of failure.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No quantitative statistics are cited.
- **Studies or research referenced:** HL7 International recommendations are referenced, but no external studies are cited.
- **Examples provided:** SHN describes its Delaware deployment model, N-by-1 network architecture, and endpoint directory/routing layer as examples of common infrastructure; it also gives examples of decentralized credential and key-directory trust models used in other sectors.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Impacted payers, EHR vendors, third-party application developers, network operators, providers, patients, state Medicaid programs, smaller payers, and security/trust framework participants.
- **Economic implications:** SHN argues endpoint directory infrastructure and common rails would reduce duplicative manual connection work and administrative waste; it characterizes payer reporting burden as minimal relative to ecosystem benefits.
- **Technical feasibility:** SHN views FHIR PA implementation, FAST NDH endpoint directories, and FAST Security outcomes as feasible, while recommending flexibility for decentralized architectures.
- **Patient care impact:** Faster electronic PA, real-time status visibility, and complete drug/non-drug PA data across patient/provider/payer APIs could reduce delays and improve patient-centered control over information.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive
- **Tone:** Technical, collaborative, and infrastructure-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "We therefore strongly support CMS's proposal" - Context: SHN's position on requiring CRD and DTR, with PAS added.
2. "There is no principled reason to process this request through fax, portal, or phone" - Context: SHN's support for medical benefit drug PA through FHIR APIs.
3. "The absence of a centralized, authoritative, machine-readable directory of payer API endpoints" - Context: SHN's rationale for API endpoint reporting.
4. "The Case for Technology-Neutral, Outcomes-Based Adoption" - Context: SHN's recommendation on FAST Security and alternative trust architectures.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - SHN recommends shifting the compliance date to end of Q1 2028 and clarifying January 1, 2028 version convergence.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment argues common endpoint infrastructure reduces duplicative implementation work and administrative waste.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - SHN devotes a major section to organizational identity, authorization, revocation, OAuth, certificates, and alternative trust models.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - SHN provides detailed implementation views on FHIR APIs, endpoint metadata, security topology, and directory operation.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - SHN discusses maturity of CRD, DTR, PAS, NCPDP SCRIPT, RTPB, FAST NDH, and FAST Security.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - SHN links electronic PA to faster decisions, patient status visibility, and patient-centered data control.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment emphasizes common rails connecting payers, providers, EHR vendors, apps, and network operators.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - SHN supports claims-processing system categorization and asks for guidance on edge cases.
